name: March First Movement
info: The March First Movement was a series of largely peaceful protests against Japanese colonial rule, held throughout Korea and by the Korean diaspora from 1 March 1919, which met violent suppression and led to the Korean Provisional Government.

facts.where: Korea, from Seoul to all thirteen provinces and Jeju Island; Manchuria, the Russian Far East, Hawaii and Philadelphia among the Korean diaspora.
facts.period: Planned in late 1918 and early 1919; protests from 1 March 1919, concentrated in March and April; related protests continued until 1921.
facts.figures: The thirty-three signers of the Korean Declaration of Independence, among them the Cheondoist leaders Kwŏn Tongjin, O Se-chang and Son Byong-hi; the missionary Frank Schofield; the student Yu Gwan-sun.
facts.outcome: Korea was not liberated promptly, but the Korean Provisional Government was founded, Japan's colonial government granted some limited cultural freedoms known as cultural rule, and the movement became central to Korean national memory.

t: The movement began on 1 March 1919 with a public reading of the Korean Declaration of Independence in Seoul and spread within weeks to all thirteen provinces, in around 1,500 to 1,800 protests.

Organisers chose nonviolence and turned to international opinion, but the protests were frequently violently suppressed; one Korean estimate of 1920 claimed 7,509 deaths and 46,948 arrests, while Japanese authorities reported lower numbers.
It did not free Korea, but it led to the Korean Provisional Government and to cultural rule, and it inspired other movements abroad, though how far is debated.
dyk: The Canadian missionary Frank Schofield, who documented the protests and publicised them abroad, has since been described as the “Thirty-fourth Representative”, equating his significance to that of the thirty-three signers of the declaration.
ev: Japan formally annexes Korea and begins a process of forced cultural assimilation
After the end of the First World War, Woodrow Wilson announces the Fourteen Points, including national self-determination
Former emperor Gojong dies on 21 January, and Koreans widely suspect that Japan poisoned him
Students in Japan proclaim a declaration of independence in February and are arrested en masse
Signers read the Korean Declaration of Independence at T’aehwagwan on 1 March, and a crowd at Tapgol Park begins a march along Jongno
In the Jeamni massacre on 15 April, Japanese authorities lure 20 to 30 civilians into a church, shoot them and burn it down
Korean exiles in Shanghai found the Korean Provisional Government in April
South Korea designates 1 March as the national holiday Samiljeol

sections.background:
In 1910, Japan formally annexed Korea. Its rule was at first especially tight: Japan took control of Korea’s economy and began a process of Japanisation, forced cultural assimilation. Land was confiscated from Koreans and given to Japanese people, and economic and administrative systems were created that were systemically discriminatory. Resistance was violently suppressed, and freedom of speech and press were tightly controlled. Koreans had to send growing portions of their output to Japan for what was seen as inadequate compensation, and the quality of life of many farmers and labourers declined. There were 6 strikes with 362 participants in 1916, 8 with 1,128 in 1917 and 50 with 4,442 in 1918, which historians of the National Institute of Korean History take as a sign of rising discontent.

After the First World War ended in 1918, United States President Woodrow Wilson announced the Fourteen Points, which included the right of national self-determination, and Koreans who learned of them interpreted them as support for their independence movement. Scholars debate Wilson’s sincerity: some argue that his advocacy was limited to the former colonies of the defeated Central Powers, while Ku Daeyeol argues that it was sincere but frustrated by geopolitical realities. The colonial government suppressed discussion of the Fourteen Points.

Koreans made several unsuccessful attempts to be represented at the Paris Peace Conference. On 21 January 1919 the former emperor Gojong died suddenly, and Koreans widely suspected that Japan had poisoned him, although Japan reported natural causes. Public outrage at the possibility of murder has been evaluated as critical to the timing of the movement.
sections.aims:
The movement sought Korea’s independence from Japanese rule through nonviolent resistance and by turning international public opinion against Japan. In late 1918 the leaders of the native Korean religion Cheondoism, among them Kwŏn Tongjin, O Se-chang and Son Byong-hi, reached a consensus that this approach would be effective. They agreed that they needed help from other major groups in Korea, and sent representatives to secure the cooperation of politicians and organisations.

An earlier statement came from Korean students in Japan, who by the mid-1910s had been exposed to liberal democracy, partly through the Japanese Taishō Democracy movement and Wilson’s Fourteen Points. In February 1919, 8,600 students of the Korean Young People’s Independence Organization proclaimed a declaration of independence and sent it to the Japanese government and to attendees of the Paris Peace Conference. The students were arrested en masse, though news of their act reached Korea.

The Korean Declaration of Independence, signed by thirty-three representatives from 25 to 27 February, contains the text “We entertain no spirit of vengeance towards Japan... [L]et there be no violence”. The organizers also sent copies to the Korean diaspora, to President Wilson and to participants in the Paris Peace Conference. They had meant to start in Tapgol Park in Seoul, but worried that angered onlookers might retaliate violently if the leaders were arrested there, so they moved the start, in the interest of nonviolence, to the less visible restaurant T’aehwagwan.
sections.events:
Around noon on 1 March 1919, the day of Gojong’s public funeral, 29 of the 33 signers gathered at T’aehwagwan and read the declaration. The restaurant owner An Sunhwan reported the event to the Japanese Government-General of Chōsen, and about 80 military police arrested the signers. Meanwhile 4,000 to 5,000 people had assembled at Tapgol Park, where around 2 p.m. an unidentified young man read the declaration aloud. The crowd cheered for Korean independence and marched onto the street Jongno, and by the time it reached the Daehanmun gate of Deoksugung palace it numbered tens of thousands.

That day protests were also held in Pyongyang, Chinnamp’o, Anju and Wonsan, cities linked to Seoul by railway. By 19 March all thirteen provinces had hosted protests, Jeju Island held its first on 21 March, and all but seven of the 218 administrative districts took part. Protests often coincided with market days and were often held at government offices. Statistics are uncertain: around 1,500 to 1,800 protests with 0.8 to 2 million participants, in a population of around 16 to 17 million. A Japanese police report claimed 1,214 protests with 1.1 million participants.

Koreans abroad joined. In Manchuria a large protest was held in Longjing on 13 March, with estimates of 20,000 to 30,000 people, and Japanese pressure on the warlord Zhang Zuolin led to around 17 to 19 deaths. Protests followed in Ussuriysk and in Sinhanch’on in Vladivostok, and Koreans in Hawaii and Philadelphia held meetings.
sections.people:
Thirty-three representatives signed the declaration. Cheondoist leaders began the planning and secured alliances with major Christian and Buddhist groups and student organisations, and with some former officials of the Korean Empire, though the Joseon-era politicians Park Yung-hyo and Han Kyu-sŏl rebuffed them. Eleven of the 33 signers were from the Pyongan region. Presbyterian leaders in Pyongyang had independently planned a protest, and their efforts were merged into the Cheondoist ones.

The protests were broadly supported by merchants, noblemen, literati, kisaeng, labourers, monks, Christians, Cheondoists, students and farmers. According to one estimate, 17% of those arrested were Christians, who made up less than 1% of the population, 58.4% were peasants and 3.9% were labourers. Women both led and joined many protests, and a group of female students wrote a public letter, “From Korean School Girls”, to world leaders. The 16-year-old Ewha Haktang student Yu Gwan-sun, who spread news of the protests through villages around Cheonan, was arrested and died of her injuries in Seodaemun Prison on 28 September 1920; she is remembered in South Korea as a martyr.

Foreigners took part too. Robert Grierson allowed secret meetings in his house in Sŏngjin, and Frank Schofield was asked to document the protests. The journalist Valentine S. McClatchy and the missionary Homer Hulbert publicised them in the United States, and Korean-American activists such as Henry Chung did the same. Syngman Rhee and Chung were refused permission to travel to Paris, and Kim Kyu-sik went with the Chinese delegation.
sections.outcomes:
The Government-General had not expected the protests and was surprised by their scale. It recruited firemen and railroad guards, and received more military police, police officers and army divisions from Japan, equipped with lethal weapons. There are numerous reports of authorities opening fire or conducting bayonet charges on unarmed protestors. At Suwon and Anseong they reportedly burnt 276 homes, killed 29 and arrested around 2,000 people. On 15 April, in the Jeamni massacre, they lured 20 to 30 civilians into a church, opened fire and burned it down to hide the killings. There are reports of torture, executions and harsh prison conditions in Seodaemun Prison.

The numbers are disputed. One Korean estimate of 1920 claimed 7,509 deaths and 46,948 arrests. Japanese officials reported 553 people killed and more than 12,000 arrested from 1 March to 11 April. The historian Kwon Tae-eok argued that Japanese sources were incentivised to lower the numbers. The South Korean National Institute of Korean History’s database of 2019 gives deliberately conservative estimates.

The movement did not bring prompt liberation. Japan ran a disinformation campaign, denying the protests, portraying them as violent Bolshevik uprisings or blaming missionaries, and no major foreign government challenged Japanese rule. The colonial government did grant limited cultural freedoms, grouped as “cultural rule”, including permission for Korean newspapers such as The Dong-A Ilbo and The Chosun Ilbo. Commentators called these changes largely cosmetic; Michael Shin argues that colonial authority actually expanded, and by the late 1930s many concessions were retracted.
sections.legacy:
The legacy of the movement is still actively debated by scholars. It invigorated the Korean independence movement, and Koreans who fled repression, many of them to Shanghai, founded the Korean Provisional Government in April 1919, now considered a predecessor of the government of South Korea. Michael Shin views the movement as a turning point for Korean nationalism, from elite leadership to popular action. The 1926 June Tenth Movement had many similar protest actions.

The movement is widely seen in South Korea as a landmark in the formation of modern Korean national identity, and the constitution’s first sentence mentions the “March First Independence Movement of 1919”. South Korea designated 1 March a national holiday in 1949. North Korea made it a holiday in 1946, later demoted it, and teaches that Kim Il Sung’s family took the lead, an account that downplays the figures who later became influential in South Korea. Scholars in both North and South largely agree that the movement was unlikely to lead to prompt liberation.

Its effect on other movements is debated. Fu Ssu-nien and other organizers of China’s May Fourth Movement cited it as an inspiration, and Gandhi is reported to have read of the protests and returned to India to launch non-cooperation. Some historians note that these protests arose from different causes. Youngseo Baik argues that the movement can be considered a revolution. In August 2015 the former Japanese prime minister Yukio Hatoyama apologised at Seodaemun Prison for the treatment of its prisoners.

summary: The March First Movement was a wave of mostly peaceful protests against Japanese rule in Korea, begun on 1 March 1919 with a reading of the Korean Declaration of Independence. It was violently suppressed and did not free Korea, but it led to the Korean Provisional Government and to cultural rule.
references: Erez Manela, The Wilsonian Moment: Self-Determination and the International Origins of Anticolonial Nationalism (Oxford University Press, 2007)
Michael Shin, Korean National Identity under Japanese Colonial Rule: Yi Gwangsu and the March First Movement of 1919 (Routledge, 2018)
Frank Baldwin, The March First Movement: Korean Challenge and Japanese Response (Columbia University Press, 1972)
notes: The article gives the signers' meetings as 25 to 27 February and printing on 27 February; used as written.
Casualty and participant figures are the article's ranges and attributed estimates (Korean estimate of 1920; Japanese report); no single figure is chosen.
The article does not state when the movement's related protests began to wind down beyond 'until 1921', so end is 1921.
The Gandhi claim is given with 'reportedly' as in the article.
